item.title: Recognised After Death: Feminist Readings Of Nandita K.S. And Emily Dickinson’s Poetry
item.description: Death certainly becomes a site of resistance against everything that left them unheard in their lives and in their poems. The post Recognised After Death: Feminist Readings Of Nandita K.S. And Emily Dickinson’s Poetry appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: “Boy Trapper” To Boycott: Why India Still Punishes Love In 2026
item.description: In India, the harsh reaction to love marriages transgressing religion, caste and class divisions, shows how deeply entrenched endogamy is. The post “Boy Trapper” To Boycott: Why India Still Punishes Love In 2026 appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: Algorithmic Inequalities: How AI Hiring Tools Replicate Old Workplace Biases
item.description: AI-powered hiring tools are deeply embroiled in exacerbating existing inequalities in the labour market. The post Algorithmic Inequalities: How AI Hiring Tools Replicate Old Workplace Biases appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: In Search Of A Room Of One’s Own: Reading Zeenath Sajida And Virginia Woolf
item.description: The room that Virginia Woolf, Zeenath Sajida and thousands of other women speak of is a metaphor for every opportunity and resource that women have been denied and deprived of. The post In Search Of A Room Of One’s Own: Reading Zeenath Sajida And Virginia Woolf appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: What Charlotte Brontë’s ‘Villette’ Can Teach Us About Women, Independence, And Refusing To Settle
item.description: Charlotte Brontë's 'Villette' follows the journey of Lucy Snowe, who despite her quiet disposition, strives for an independent life. The post What Charlotte Brontë’s ‘Villette’ Can Teach Us About Women, Independence, And Refusing To Settle appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: When Home Isn’t Safe: The Ghaziabad Sisters And The Violence We Don’t Name
item.description: The Ghaziabad suicides were not about phone addiction but about three children who faced the most ignored form of abuse within their natal family. The post When Home Isn’t Safe: The Ghaziabad Sisters And The Violence We Don’t Name appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: Unhinged Women In Fiction And Why Women Just Can’t Get Enough Of Them
item.description: In many ways, these new heroines are the spiritual descendants of the madwoman, but this time, they’re telling their own stories. The post Unhinged Women In Fiction And Why Women Just Can’t Get Enough Of Them appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: Notes On The ‘Uses Of The Erotic’: Experiencing The Erotic As Feminist Joy
item.description: Being in touch with the erotic and its knowledge has reiterated that joy and satisfaction in life need not hinge on societal predispositions. The post Notes On The ‘Uses Of The Erotic’: Experiencing The Erotic As Feminist Joy appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: Mostari Banu v. ECI: Redefining Feminist Citizenship And Muslim Women’s Agency Amidst SIR
item.description: The case of Mostari Banu v. ECI asserts that citizenship is not a legal-static status but the gendered and culturally mediated one. The post Mostari Banu v. ECI: Redefining Feminist Citizenship And Muslim Women’s Agency Amidst SIR appeared first on Feminism in India.

item.title: Queer Desire and Female Friendship in Simone de Beauvoir’s The Inseparables
item.description: 'The Inseparables' becomes a fertile ground to dig for resonances of ambiguity and ambivalence between queer friendships, lesbian and/or asexual romances, and platonic love affairs. The post Queer Desire and Female Friendship in Simone de Beauvoir’s The Inseparables appeared first on Feminism in India.
